en: The Sūtra of the Divine Incantation of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmamitra of Jibin during the Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was dwelling on Mount Kharānta, at the abode of the Rishi Saṃbodhi.
At that place, together with a great assembly of countless bhikṣu śrāvakas,
and also with immeasurable asaṃkhyeya bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he had already expounded the Tathāgata-guṇa-sūtra.
At that time, a wish-fulfilling jewel appeared in the western direction, adorned on all sides by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Śakrābhilagna jewels.

The radiance of this precious gem eclipsed all other colors and lights; only the Tathāgata and the wish-fulfilling jewel were visible, while the other immeasurable, boundless, and ineffable colors appeared like empty space, and the majestic light of the Tathāgata became even more brilliant.

This assembly of followers did not perceive their own bodies, nor did they see one another; all forms of the great multitude were extinguished without remainder, no longer confronting the eyes. They could neither apprehend physical bodies nor tactile objects; wherever they looked, they saw only empty space. They did not even see the sun, moon, or stars, nor the elements of earth, water, fire, or wind, as these did not confront the eyes. Their ears heard no sounds, and their noses smelled no fragrances. There was no mind or mental factors, no sense of self or what belongs to self, and no arising of perceptions regarding the six sense bases. As they gazed toward other directions, they perceived no gross elements; in every location, they saw only the Buddha’s body, its marks, and its radiance.
Furthermore, from afar they beheld a wish-fulfilling jewel, surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *śakrābhilagna* jewels as its adornment, and nothing else was seen.

In this assembly, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwelling on the ten stages who had attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and were in their final existence as those destined for Buddhahood in one more birth; seeing such signs, they were not startled, terrified, or afraid, for they understood that all dharmas are empty, having the nature of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), and therefore they were not startled, not terrified, and not afraid.

The other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kiṃnaras, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, humans, and non-humans who were present in the assembly were utterly struck with terror and fear, giving rise to sorrow. Their minds were obscured by darkness and thrown into agitation; they could no longer see one another, and there was no place where they could seek refuge. What was the cause of this?
"For what cause and condition is this so? By whose power is it?
At that time, there was among the assembly a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Brahmadatta, who joined his palms toward the Buddha and spoke these verses:
"The nature of all phenomena is suchness, yet no one knows it;
dwelling in reliance upon the aggregate of form, the six sense faculties are shrouded in darkness.
Failing to see even a single aggregate, they contemplate and seek after the aggregate of form."
Those who harbor doubts regarding the Buddha-dharma—such persons exist within this assembly.
As it is here, so it is there; they universally understand the nature of space.
Courageous and steadfast in that samādhi, their bodies are ineffable.
The great wish-fulfilling jewel is seen upon his crown;
the Śakrābhilagna jewels are all seen from afar by him.
This being of great wisdom has crossed over the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
All those of great wisdom desire to come and see the World-Honored One;
now that the profound Dharma is being preached, they are certain to have no doubts.
To comfort this assembly, let them all come to take refuge in the World-Honored One.
"The sphere of activity of the courageous and steadfast is to teach and transform sentient beings until they are matured.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"It is just as you have said; such is the sphere of activity of those in samādhi."
If one hears of the place of right abiding, This is where sentient beings of wisdom dwell.
This is the treasury of space, The sphere of action for Bodhisattvas;
Without dependence and without conceptual proliferation— That is the manifestation of samādhi.
Sentient beings are attached to two views, And are constantly plundered by them;
Attached to the two views of annihilationism and eternalism, They are perpetually obscured from both sides.
If those with such dualistic views Desire to attain liberation, [they must abandon them].
Its nature is ineffable, and one swiftly realizes the various stages (*bhūmi*).

"Furthermore, son of good family, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who has first resolved upon awakening describes the characteristics of the initial stage as being the six *pāramitās*, up to knowing the reality of the arising and ceasing of the great elements. Thereafter, he knows that all phenomena are ineffable, devoid of intrinsic nature, without arising and without ceasing, without objective domain, unmoving and unshakable."
Thus they practice all deeds;

thus they completely abandon the two views of annihilationism and eternalism without giving rise to fear; they do not give rise to a mind that perceives objects within any phenomena, swiftly attaining the full perfection of the six pāramitās;
and they no longer abide within the views of annihilationism or eternalism.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the entire great assembly saw, heard, perceived, and knew him according to his true form and appearance.
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his right arm and spoke these words:
“The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha is coming.”
Having spoken these words, he addressed the great assembly, saying: "This Bodhisattva has attained samādhis like the great ocean;

he upholds the Bodhisattva precepts like Mount Sumeru; his wisdom that penetrates all things is like space; his diligent application of vigor is like a swift wind; his cultivation of patience is like a vajra; his insight is like the void; and among all Bodhisattvas, he is like a supreme banner."
It is the guide for those heading toward nirvāṇa; it is the treasury of all roots of goodness;
it is the vessel obtained by the poor;
and it is the sun for those entering the darkness.
For those who have lost their way, it is the moon;
for those who are terrified, it is Mount Sumeru;
for those scorched by the heat of afflictions, it is the nectar of immortality.
It is the seed-bed for all roots of goodness;
it is the bridge for those proceeding toward great nirvana;
it is the boat for those fallen into the evil realms and the ladder for those born in the heavens.
He is a savior for those who slander and use harsh speech;
a canopy for those afflicted by the heat of suffering.
Among all non-Buddhists, he is like a lion king.
It encompasses all views like water and a mirror;
it is armor against the enemy Māra and medicine for those who violate the precepts;
it is the ground for practicing all roots of goodness and the flowers for one who weaves garlands.
A treasury for those who practice;
exquisite garments for those lacking shame and modesty;
and a skilled physician for the sick.
Food for the hungry;
the moon-jewel for the thirsty;
a bed for those exhausted by fatigue.
It is the day for those practicing the correct cultivation of samādhi;
it is the great chariot for those heading toward bodhi;
it is the supreme ground for those roaming in dhyāna and samādhi.
The jewel wheel is that which assists awakening.
"Good son! This is the fruit of one who is directed toward the perfections."
This son of good family is a wish-fulfilling jewel for those who advance in the practice of the ten stages;
this son of good family is a pārijātaka tree for those who advance in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi;
he is a sword that severs the fetters of false views, a diamond-like shatterer of all habitual tendencies, and a sublime skillful means capable of subduing all Māras.
It is that which awakens the mind;
it is the basis upon which all the Buddha-dharmas rely;
it is the flower-garland of the pratyekabuddhas, the robe of the śrāvakas, the eyes of the devas, and the true path of humanity.
He is the refuge for animals, the protector of hungry ghosts, and the honored savior of those in hell;
he is the field of merit for all sentient beings;
he is the great vehicle of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
This son of good family is the supreme minister of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the three periods of time, guarding the gate of the city of the Dharma.
This son of good family is even fully adorned with the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) and has attained the complete perfection of the Buddha’s wisdom.
This son of good family is worthy of offerings from all sentient beings; with the exception of the Tathāgata himself, he is the most supreme among all other those worthy of offerings.
“O great assembly! You should all revere him;
each according to your capacity, you should prepare offerings, making them with devotion, respect, and honor.

With various precious jewels, banners, pennants, and jeweled canopies; with ointments, powdered incense, robes, necklaces, and various miscellaneous items; and by cleaning and adorning the roads in many ways, you should praise him with various hymns of praise. All of you shall, before long, become vessels for these merits.”

At that time, the entire great assembly, being in perfect harmony, rose from their seats and turned toward the direction where the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja had appeared. With palms joined in reverence, their hearts filled with joy and their countenances serene, they gazed upon him with pure eyes.

At that time, the great bodhisattvas, the great śrāvakas, the lords of the devas, the lords of the nāgas, the lords of the yakṣas, the lords of the asuras, the lords of the garuḍas, the lords of the kiṃnaras, the lords of the mahoragas, and the rishis possessing the five supernatural powers, each had this thought:
"What kind of most supreme and excellent offerings should we provide to honor this son of good family?"

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha transformed the Sahā world so that its ground became as level as the palm of a hand and adorned with the seven treasures. He removed all mountains, wildernesses, mounds, walls, rubble, ashes, dung, foul odors, dust, mist, clouds, thunder, and the sounds of gandharvas. All trees were transformed into the seven treasures, becoming fully endowed with flowers, leaves, fruits, and fragrances; even the roots, branches, joints, stems, and leaves of the vegetation upon the earth were likewise transformed into the seven treasures.

Throughout the entire Sahā world, all illnesses were eliminated; all beings in the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts were freed from all suffering and affliction, and all obtained clothing, food, drink, and ornaments.

All sentient beings within this Sahā world shall attain wondrous and exquisite physical forms that are upright and majestic; they shall possess supreme majesty and virtue with all limbs complete; they shall eliminate all fetters and afflictions so that their minds attain tranquility; their hearts shall take delight in all roots of goodness, and with pure minds, they shall abide securely in the Triple Gem.

In this assembled multitude, transformational wish-fulfilling jewels spontaneously appeared in both hands; from each and every wish-fulfilling jewel, light radiated forth, illuminating this Sahā world everywhere.
Furthermore, that precious jewel emitted exquisite and joyful sounds, raining down various kinds of jewels, various kinds of wonderful garments, and various kinds of necklaces;
it rained down various kinds of golden chain necklaces and pearl necklaces;
and it also rained down various kinds of exquisite flowers—blue lotuses, red lotuses, crimson lotuses, white lotuses, and water-stone flowers.
Furthermore, they rained down *tāmālapatra* incense and powdered *gośīrṣa-candana* sandalwood to adorn the path.

On both sides of the road, they manifested pavilions made of the seven treasures like those of Śakra; within these pavilions, they manifested various celestial maidens like the Queen of Māra, who performed the five kinds of music and enjoyed themselves in pleasure.

Above the Buddha, in the midst of the void, he manifested a celestial jewel canopy extending for a hundred *yojanas*, adorned with exquisite, pure, and fresh jeweled nets, and hung with strings of genuine pearls as ornaments within it. He produced various musical performances that surpassed those of the heavens; from the fields, grasses, trees, forests, flowers, leaves, and all manner of fruits, each emitted wondrous sounds far exceeding celestial music. Those who heard these sounds attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, the entire great assembly, beholding such magnificent adornments performed by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganagañja, attained what they had never experienced before and thought to themselves:
"How shall we prepare a seat for this virtuous man before the World-Honored One?"

At that time, a precious lotus flower appeared before the Buddha, with a stem of white silver, leaves of gold, a pedestal of agate, and filaments made of Brahma-maṇi jewels; it was ten li in length and breadth.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of such precious lotus flowers surrounding it on all sides. [The assembly] saw the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja suddenly sitting cross-legged upon the flower, and they saw the wish-fulfilling jewel atop his head. They also saw the retinue brought by Gaganagañja, each likewise seated upon the pedestals of other lotus flowers.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja in verse:
“As all those who have come before, the Bodhisattvas of great renown,
Reverently prostrate to the World-Honored One, And only then take their seats.”
"This noble man has come, manifesting great adornments;
yet he did not pay homage to the World-Honored One, and suddenly we see him already seated.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja replied to the Bodhisattva Maitreya in verse:
"To see these great beings, who dwell well within the Buddha-dharma;
to not perceive sentient beings, and to not rely on any conceptualization.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva again spoke in verse:
"If you do not perceive sentient beings and abide in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi),
for what purpose do you adorn [the world]?
Please explain this to me."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja replied again in verse:
"This skillful means is courageous and robust, For the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings;
Yet ordinary people, ignorant of the ultimate truth, Proceed with the deluded thoughts of the mundane."
"Those who are wise regarding conventional truth, yet suffer because they are deluded about the ultimate,
manifest such adornments in order to liberate them. At that time,
the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!

This good man is as you have described: even if all ordinary worldlings were unable to know the sphere of liberation of a single *srotāpanna*, and even if all sentient beings were to attain the stage of *srotāpanna*, they would still be unable to know the sphere of liberation of a single *sakṛdāgāmin*.
All *srotāpannas*, *sakṛdāgāmins*, *anāgāmins*, and *arhats* likewise do not know the sphere of liberation and practice of even a single *pratyekabuddha*.

All sentient beings who have become solitary *pratyekabuddhas*, like lone white stallions, likewise do not know the skillful means and virtuous conduct of a single *bodhisattva-mahāsattva* who has attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and teaches and transforms sentient beings.

All sentient beings who have attained the patience of non-arising do not know the practice of liberation according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of a single *bodhisattva-mahāsattva* who has attained the *śūraṅgama-samādhi* and unimpeded eloquence.
“Good son! This Ākāśagarbha has attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), has attained unimpeded eloquence (*asaṅga-pratibhāna*), and has attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.

He knows the roots of goodness within the minds of this great assembly throughout incalculable eons; it is because he should manifest great adornments and because he dwells in the stage of detachment from desire.”
This son of good family has vanished from the western direction and come here!

He manifests in common with all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas by entering the samādhi of the immeasurable sphere of empty space and displaying supernatural powers, causing all sentient beings to give rise to a sense of wonder;
furthermore, he manifests adornments within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) in order to teach and transform immeasurable sentient beings.

If these good sons manifest the adornment of non-arising according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), then even gods and humans shall be struck with alarm, confusion, and loss of mind; even Bodhisattvas up to the eighth stage shall likewise lose their minds. No one will be able to perceive the characteristics of their conduct as they enter such profound dharmas of merit.

This good son well understands skillful means; he has crossed the ocean of all Buddha-dharmas and severed all doubt and confusion. Naturally and skillfully knowing the crossings of all expedient means, he stands like a royal banner among all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

“Good son! This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha demonstrates to all sentient beings the path to the heavenly realms and the path to Nirvāṇa; he is able to untie the knots of afflictions and the maladies of the mind, and he also cures the various ailments of increase and decrease within the body composed of the four great elements.”

If there are sentient beings oppressed by various wrong views, who are lost in the wilderness of birth and death and do not know the skillful means—how can they be called the path to the heavens or the path to nirvāṇa?
"O sentient beings!

If you invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, pay homage, and make offerings by burning various kinds of incense, these sons of good family will perceive the roots of goodness in their own minds that were obscured by the fetters of their views;

they will also come to know the seeds of roots of goodness planted in their past minds, as well as the merit of practicing generosity and upholding the precepts through their present offerings to the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha."

Through such means as these, they may manifest the path of rectitude through skillful means within dreams; by the power of such skillful means, their minds attain liberation from all evil views, evil deeds, evil vows, evil pursuits, evil refuges, and evil destinies.

Their conduct of body, speech, and mind is entirely upright; their aspirations are upright; they draw near to upright and true spiritual friends; and they swiftly attain liberation from the fetters of foul odors and the diseases of evil views.

Because their aspirations are virtuous and they practice virtuous deeds, they quickly achieve mastery over the mind and abide in profound patience. They swiftly bring an end to the evil karma of the miserable realms.

"If there are sentient beings whose bodies are oppressed by various ailments and whose minds are distracted; who are deaf, blind, mute, or deficient in their faculties; whose limbs are deformed or who exhibit the signs of approaching death."

Regarding such matters as these, one should single-mindedly recite the name of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha; for the sake of eliminating all illnesses and desiring freedom from disease, one should burn aloeswood incense, solid black aloeswood, or tagara incense, and pay homage to Ākāśagarbha.

This virtuous great man appears before that person in a night dream, manifesting in the form of a brahmin, or appearing as a Śākya, the goddess Mahāgaurī, the goddess Mañjughoṣā, a kṣatriya, a minister, a military official, a skilled physician, or in the form of a parent, or a son or daughter. Appearing thus before the sick person in a night dream, he explains various medicinal decoctions according to the specific illness; once the patient has taken them, all afflictions are completely eliminated.

Furthermore, regarding whatever matters they may seek—whether it be the desire for extensive learning, the desire for tranquility, the desire to cultivate dhyāna and attain wisdom, the desire for a good reputation, the desire to seek craftsmanship, or the desire to attain mastery—[he provides guidance].
Desiring exquisite physical form; desiring fiefdoms; desiring power; desiring talent;
desiring a beautiful voice; desiring offspring; desiring a retinue; desiring merit;
desiring generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; desiring eloquent speech; desiring that others...
With reverence, they desire to be liberated from all evils and to abide securely in generosity, up to and including wisdom; they desire to obtain long life;
they desire to obtain various necessary requisites and, having obtained them, to be able to utilize them; they desire to exhort the stingy to practice giving;
they desire to cause those who have broken the precepts to abide securely in the observance of the precepts; and they desire to cause those who are indolent to abide securely in diligence.
Desiring to exhort the ignorant to abide in wisdom, he exhorts those who have not yet fixed upon a vehicle to abide as Śrāvakas,
and exhorts those who have already embraced their own vehicle to abide as Pratyekabuddhas.
This son of good family employs such skillful means to demonstrate this to all sentient beings.
"If there are sentient beings who abandon great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), protecting their own bodies and minds while forsaking other beings— if such a mind exists,

by what skillful means (*upāya*) can I exhort those people to cause them to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, to dwell securely in the four Brahma-abodes (*brahmavihāra*) of skillful means, and even lead them to abide in great compassion?"

This person pays homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha—whether in a forest hermitage, within a grove, or in the open air—burning aloeswood incense, solid black aloeswood, or tagara incense. With a sincere heart, they join their palms, prostrate themselves with the five limbs touching the ground, and universally pay homage to the ten directions.
At that time, they should recite these dharani phrases: *Amṛteśa amṛteśa kāruṇika (1) cara cara (2)*
Vigatāre samamaṅkha rucamānagārunika 4. Cendāmani purayika gārunika 5.
Sarva-aśami-tāra-va-re (6) ācintāri (7) bhañja-bhañja (8)
1. Lūci pippikā-cūḍe 2. Pippikā-kāruṇike 3. Pūrṇeśvarā-māśe 4. 11.

*Sattvapatrāśca-aśoka-kṛte svāhā.* (12) “This son of good family, for the sake of those people, manifests the form of a human, the form of a deer, the form of a horse, or the form of a deva; according to their merits, he manifests such forms and speaks to show them a single skillful means.”

By means of these skillful methods, they are able to transform and guide immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of sentient beings—those of indeterminate vehicle, those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, and those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle—enabling them, within a single moment, the brief duration of a finger-snap, through slight skillful wisdom, to dwell securely in the unimpeded Mahāyāna and attain non-retrogression;
furthermore, they cause them to attain various samādhis and dhāraṇīs, as well as to attain patience and dwell in the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
"This is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha!
He has accomplished such inconceivable power of skillful means, wisdom, and great compassion. Good son!"

Even if one were able to reach the very limits of space, there would be no one capable of knowing the power of this son of good family’s wisdom, skillful means, great kindness, great compassion, and samādhi, nor anyone who could reach the limit of his teaching and transforming of sentient beings.
This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha has accomplished such inconceivable and boundless merit.

"Good son! If there are sentient beings who are free from flattery, deception, and delusion, who possess correct conduct and dignified demeanor, who have accomplished right view, who are upright and honest without guile, who do not praise themselves, who are free from jealousy, and who are devoid of craftiness and possess a virtuous mind; [for them, this Bodhisattva will appear]."

For such persons as these, this son of good family feels compassion; he demonstrates the wisdom of skillful means and the vigor of correct practice. By the power of this wisdom of skillful means and the vigor of correct practice, they are liberated from all suffering and affliction, give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, dedicate all roots of goodness toward the unsurpassed path, and attain non-retrogression.
Because they fulfill the six pāramitās through the power of diligence, they proceed with great vigor and swiftly attain the unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva!
Having accomplished such inconceivable and immeasurable merit, he transforms and guides sentient beings.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason do you alone see this good man’s crown jewel as being of such exquisite color, so dignified and brilliantly radiant, unlike those of other bodhisattvas?”
The Buddha said,
“Good son! This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha has perfected great compassion and acts to benefit sentient beings by liberating them from matters of great suffering.”

If there are sentient beings who have committed root transgressions and are destined to fall into the evil realms, having severed all roots of goodness and wholesome conduct—for such sentient beings, this son of good family acts as a wondrous medicine.

If there are sentient beings who have fallen into the great darkness of ignorance, imprisoned within the dungeon of obscured and evil views, [the Buddha] acts as a great illumination like the sun, causing them to repent and sever their fundamental evils, and being able to remove the poisonous arrows of doubt from the minds of sentient beings.

There may be sentient beings who have shattered the vessel of their minds by committing root transgressions; having lost all wholesome dharmas, they are destined for the evil realms, without refuge or destination, and abandoned by all clear wisdom. This son of good family can show these beings—shrouded in the darkness of sin—the way to the wholesome path, like a precious staff;
he can also wash away all foul-smelling fetters and afflictions, turn them away from the evil realms and settle them among humans and devas, leading them to the bliss of nirvana like a great chariot.

If there are sentient beings who are driven by excessive desire, or who possess extreme anger and a distracted mind, or who are shrouded by much ignorance and delusion; who deny cause and effect, fail to see, feel no dread for, and have no fear of future lives; and who, insatiable in their craving for wealth, constantly commit the ten types of unwholesome actions—then for such beings, this son of good family acts like a great vehicle that closes off the evil realms and establishes them among gods and humans, leading them to the bliss of Nirvana.
For this reason, all devas and humans should make offerings to these sons of good family, with the sole exception of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is called a fundamental offense?”

Once sentient beings have committed these root offenses, they sever all roots of goodness and conduct and shall fall into the evil realms; because they have committed these root offenses leading to downfall, they are deprived of all the happiness of humans and devas.
Furthermore, by means of this son of good family, those sentient beings are enabled to fully possess the happiness of humans, devas, and nirvāṇa.
The Buddha said:
"Good son! There are five matters by which an anointed Kṣatriya king commits a root transgression."

Once an anointed Kṣatriya king has committed the five root transgressions, all the roots of goodness previously planted will be utterly destroyed; because he has committed these fundamental downfalls, he is separated from all the joys of humans and devas and shall fall into the evil realms.
What are these five?
Son of good family,
if an anointed kṣatriya should plunder the property of a stūpa;
If one seizes property belonging to the Sangha or property belonging to the *caitya* Sangha—whether taking it oneself or causing another to take it—this is called the first fundamental grave offense.

If, for the sake of slandering the Dharma, one hears that the Buddha has taught for the sake of *śrāvakas*, for the sake of *pratyekabuddhas*, or for the sake of the Mahāyāna, and then slanders and obstructs it so as not to allow its circulation, this is called committing the second fundamental grave offense.

"If one causes someone who has gone forth for my sake—having shaved off their hair and beard and donned the *kāṣāya*—whether they uphold the precepts or not, whether they have broken them or not, to cast off that *kāṣāya* and be forced back into lay life; or beats their body and punishes them; or imprisons them; or takes their life—this is called the third root offense."
"If a Kṣatriya king, by the power of his sovereignty, commits one of the five crimes of immediate retribution (ānantarya) or encourages others to commit the five crimes of immediate retribution,
and thus commits even one such crime among the five, this is called the fourth root transgression."

"If a Kṣatriya king asserts that there is no cause and effect and denies the next world, practices the ten unwholesome actions, and encourages many sentient beings to commit the ten unwholesome deeds, this is called the fifth root transgression."

“Good son! If a consecrated king commits even one of these five root grave offenses, he will destroy all past roots of goodness, fall into a grave offense of transgression, be separated from all the happiness of humans and devas, and shall surely fall into the evil realms.”

For this reason, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja manifests birth in frontier regions; he may manifest the appearance, clothing, and deportment of a śramaṇa, or the appearance, clothing, and deportment of a brāhmaṇa.
Manifesting his birth wherever it may be, in each respective place, he preaches the Dharma never before heard to the kṣatriyas.

Just as the Omniscient One has taught the profound sūtras, expounding and elucidating the dhāraṇīs and the stages of patience (kṣānti-bhūmi), by virtue of these causes and conditions, King Abhiṣeka, having felt shame and remorse for his previously committed evil and unwholesome deeds, shall refrain from committing them again; he will abide in generosity, tranquility, self-restraint, great diligence, and progress toward the Great Way.
"Furthermore, there are five matters by which a minister commits a fundamental grave offense. What are these five?
If that minister plunders the property of a stūpa, or seizes the property of the Saṃgha or the property of the Saṃgha of the four quarters, this is called the first fundamental grave offense."
"If a high minister destroys a kingdom, city, village, town, or settlement, this is called the second root transgression of a grave offense.

"If a high minister slanders the True Dharma—whether it be that which the Buddha taught for the śrāvakas, for the pratyekabuddhas, or for those practicing for omniscience—and slanders, obstructs, conceals, or hides it, this is called the third root transgression of a grave offense."

"If any ministers see a person who has left home to follow the Buddha, having shaved off their hair and beard and donned the kashaya robes—whether that person maintains the precepts or not, or whether they have broken them or not—and if they strip them of their dharma robes and force them back to lay life, or beat their body, punish them, imprison them, or even take their life, this is called the fourth root offense of a grave transgression."
“If a high minister commits any one of the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), this is called the fifth root transgression. ‘Good son!
If a high minister commits any one of these five root transgressions, he destroys all past roots of goodness, is separated from all the happiness of humans and devas, and shall fall into hell.’”

For this reason, for the sake of such beings as these, Ākāśagarbha manifests birth in the borderlands, assuming the appearance of a śramaṇa, or that of a brāhmaṇa, or even the forms of men and women, and preaches the Dharma to them.

In every place, he expounded the profound Dharma for the sake of great ministers, revealing and proclaiming various profound sūtras, dhāraṇīs, and the practice of patience, just as one who possesses all-knowledge would teach.

Having heard this, the minister felt shame and remorse for the evil karma he had created; he vowed never to commit such acts again, and settled himself in generosity, tranquility, self-restraint, and diligent application of effort, setting out upon the Great Path.
“Good son! A śrāvaka disciple who commits a root grave offense also has five matters [to consider]. What are these five?
Killing, sexual misconduct, stealing, lying, and shedding the blood of a Buddha—these are called the five root grave offenses committed by a śrāvaka.
If a śrāvaka commits any one of these root grave offenses, the arrow of doubt remains in his heart, withering his faculties, and he will certainly head toward the evil realms.

For the sake of such beings as these, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha manifests births wherever they may be; he appears in the form and deportment of a śramaṇa, or even in the likeness of a man, and preaches the Dharma for them.

This causes those seeking the vehicle of the śrāvaka to feel shame and remorse for their transgressions, so that they dare not commit them again; it establishes them in tranquility and self-mastery, leading them toward the unsurpassed Great Vehicle. "Good son!
For a son of good family who has first set out upon the Mahāyāna, there are eight grave offenses, such as those involving the root transgressions. What are these eight?

Suppose there is a sentient being who, due to the causes and conditions of evil karma, is born in an age of the five turbidities; yet, by virtue of a small amount of wholesome roots and proximity to a virtuous friend, they hear this profound and wondrous Dharma of the Mahāyāna. Because their awakening, understanding, and wholesome roots are slight, they resolve their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, but upon hearing a sūtra concerning the foremost marklessness (*animitta*), they instead provide analytical explanations for the sake of the ordinary and ignorant.

When foolish ordinary people hear this, they become terrified and fearful; they regress and lose the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, wishing instead to seek the vehicle of the *śrāvakas*. This is called the first bodhisattva who has committed the first fundamental grave offense.

Because of these transgressions, all cultivated roots of goodness are destroyed; one commits a grave offense of downfall, is separated from the bliss of gods, humans, and nirvāṇa, and having retreated from the bodhicitta, shall fall into the evil realms. Therefore, a bodhisattva, having known the minds and roots of goodness of others, should preach the Dharma as appropriate, just as one gradually crosses the great ocean, becoming ever deeper and wider.
Therefore, when Ākāśagarbha manifests his birth in that land, he assumes a form identical to theirs and preaches the Dharma for them; this is called the first root transgression.

"If a practitioner wishes to see the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha and repent for the evil offenses they have committed, they should, during the final watch of the night, burn aloeswood, solid black aloeswood, or tagara incense, and with palms joined, recite the name of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha."

According to their share of merit, these sons of good family shall see the forms and colors manifested by the Gaganagañja; whether they see his body, or a śramaṇa, or a brāhmaṇa, or various forms such as men or women, he will preach the Dharma for them. Thus, the fundamental grave offenses committed by these bodhisattvas who have first resolved upon awakening shall be immediately expiated. They will become capable of enduring the samādhi of the supreme and great skillful means, as well as patience and dhāraṇīs. Upon reaching the stage of abiding, they will be able to sever the evil paths and attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Regarding the six pāramitās, they will obtain the power of great vigor like a diamond, and they shall swiftly awaken to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"If he does not manifest his form before you, that beginner bodhisattva shall rise from his seat at the time when the morning star appears and address the star with these words:

'Homage to A-raṇa! Homage to A-raṇa, who has accomplished great compassion! Now you have first appeared in Jambudvīpa; may you protect me with your great compassion. I report my words to the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha of Great Compassion, so that he may reveal to me the skillful means within a dream tonight.'"
"For this reason, one may repent for the fundamental grave offenses committed and achieve the eye of skillful means and wisdom of the Mahāyāna.

Then, at the time when the morning star appeared during his sleep, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja manifested his physical form within the dream to cause him to repent. Once all evils had been extinguished, he immediately attained a samādhi called "Never Forgetting the Bodhicitta," whereby he dwelt well in the Mahāyāna and was endowed with the six pāramitās.
"If a beginner bodhisattva says to others:
'You are unable to practice the six pāramitās;
nor can you awaken to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
"You should quickly resolve upon the mind of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, so that you may attain liberation from birth and death.
The remainder is as stated above; this is called the second root transgression for a beginner.
"Furthermore, a beginner might say these words:
'What is the use of your diligently maintaining the precepts of discipline?

You should simply and swiftly resolve upon the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta). You should read and recite the Mahāyāna sūtras, and your evil deeds of body, speech, and mind shall become purified so that there will be no retribution for evil.'"
The rest is as explained above; this is called the third root offense for a beginner.
Furthermore, if a beginner should say these words: "You possess great virtue;
you should distance yourself from the Śrāvaka teachings—do not listen to them, do not read them, and do not explain them to others."
"You, son of good family!

You should conceal the sūtra-dharma of the śrāvakas; within the dharma of the śrāvakas, one does not attain the Mahāyāna, nor can it lead you to the ultimate limit. You should instead listen to and receive the Mahāyāna sūtras and explain them for others."
"Your various evil karmas shall be purified, and you will swiftly attain the Buddha-way.
If one accepts these words and adopts this view, both commit an offense; this is called the fourth root grave offense of a beginner bodhisattva.

"Furthermore, a beginner may engage in false speech and divisive talk, preaching the Mahāyāna with divergent thoughts using different sūtras, and for the sake of fame and gain, they uphold, read, and recite them; having heard them, they explain them extensively to others, saying:
'I know the Mahāyāna, not anyone else.'"

Seeing others obtain gain, they give rise to envy; they speak ill of others’ reputations, slandering and disparaging them, while claiming for themselves that they have attained superhuman dharmas (*uttarimanussadhamma*).

Such a person destroys [the precepts] and commits a grave offense of falling (*pārājika*); they depart from the Mahāyāna Dharma and shall fall into the evil realms, just as a person who enters the sea in search of treasure perishes when their ship founders. This beginner is likewise so; this is called the fifth root grave offense of a beginner.
"Furthermore, in the future there will be beginner bodhisattvas, whether lay or ordained, who read and recite the Vaipulya sūtras and say for the sake of gain and offerings:
'I understand this sublime Dharma; out of compassion for you, I shall explain it to you.'"

This beginner bodhisattva truly lacks the intention to benefit sentient beings; it is like a person suffering from hunger who enters a great fruit grove, abandons the various delicious fruits, eats poisonous fruit, and dies.

A beginner bodhisattva is also like this: having entered the precious grove of the Great Vehicle’s perfect enlightenment, they preach Mahāyāna sūtras for the sake of gain and fame; thus they commit a fundamental grave offense and are censured by all the wise. They should not be approached by the fourfold assembly of humans and devas; this is called the sixth fundamental grave offense of a beginner.

"Furthermore, a Kṣatriya king may have Cāṇḍāla state ministers, Cāṇḍāla officials, Cāṇḍāla military officers, or Cāṇḍāla physicians. Such deluded persons, though they personally possess wealth and jewels and practice giving, are dissolute and arrogant, and they bring ruin upon the Saṅgha. Relying on their status as royal officials, they plunder the property of the Saṅgha; this is called the seventh root offense for one who has first entered [the path]."

"Furthermore, if there are *kṣatriya-cāṇḍālas*, minister-*cāṇḍālas*, or bhikṣu-*cāṇḍālas* who harbor malice toward śramaṇas, proclaiming what is not the Dharma as the Dharma and the Dharma as not the Dharma; who abandon the sūtras and vinaya; who engage in untimely discourses on meaning; who establish regulations that are not in accordance with the Dharma; who sever the study of Prajñāpāramitā; and who harass and disturb bhikṣus—causing all śramaṇas to lose their pure faith and destroy their dignified deportment; who, while not being true śramaṇas, claim to be śramaṇas, and while not practicing true brahmacarya, claim to practice brahmacarya, thereby causing the fourfold assembly to increase their offerings [to such persons]."
Both the king’s minister and the bhikṣu incur guilt; this is called the eighth root transgression for a beginner.

When a beginner bodhisattva commits this root offense, they are no longer called a practitioner; they sever all roots of goodness, depart from the happiness of humans and devas, and shall fall into the evil realms.

“Good son! For the sake of these beings, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha assumes their forms and enters among their classes, manifesting in identical appearances and colors. He then preaches various sūtras and vinayas, such as the Śūraṅgama-samādhi, causing those who have committed offenses to repent of their evil karma and to bring their roots of goodness to fulfillment in ultimate nirvāṇa.”
"O noble son! If one prostrates to and praises the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, that person shall obtain great merit in the present life.

Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who, upon hearing the name of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, fashion his image and provide offerings, pay homage, show respect, and offer praise, making various kinds of ritual offerings."

In this person’s present life, water cannot drown them, fire cannot burn them, blades cannot wound them, and poisons cannot harm them; neither humans nor non-humans can cause them injury, nor do they suffer from illness, hunger, or thirst.

At the time of death, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha manifests various celestial forms—such as the sun, the moon, and other divine images—before them, causing all sentient beings to each see their own refuge and have their aspirations fulfilled.
He then speaks these verses: “If the wise perceive these Four Noble Truths;”
"Knowing the faults of birth and death, one crosses over the flow of all existences.
"If there are sentient beings who have deep faith in the Buddha, he immediately manifests a Buddha-body and speaks this verse:
'The wisdom of the Buddha is true; if one crosses over all existences...'"
“They shall attain realization of the Buddha-wisdom and be liberated from all suffering.
When these sentient beings approach the end of their lives, they shall behold the body of the Buddha; with deep hearts of love and joy, they shall leap for gladness.
Once their lives have ended, they will leave behind the world of the five turbidities and be born in a pure buddha-field to behold the Buddha and hear the Dharma. "Good son,
this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha has accomplished such inconceivable merit."

If you wish to increase your cultivation of various meditative concentrations and attain mastery over wisdom, you should bathe and purify yourself; then, during the latter part of the night, after prostrating to Ākāśagarbha and presenting various offerings, speak these words:
"O Greatly Compassionate One toward all sentient beings, I pray that you grant me the skillful means of mindfulness and concentration."
He then spoke these dharani phrases:

"Dān-mu-lan-na-han (1) | Ba-pa-ni-li (2) | Mao-ni-a-po-duo-li (3) | Na-na-yi (4) | Na-yi-mo-he-jia-lou-ni-jia (5) | A-no-po-yen-po-ji-ti (6) | A-jia-śa-po-ji-ti (7) | Po-ja-yen-po-ji-ti (8) | Lo-śa-ji-lil-ti (9) | A-na-mo-ji-ti (10) | Fu-to-ku-śa-ji-ti svāhā (11). He then bestowed upon that person the skillful means of mindfulness and concentration.

If one wishes to read and recite various sūtras and śāstras, one should also, at the time when the morning star appears, make offerings and prostrate to the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, and speak these words:
"O Greatly Compassionate Ākāśagarbha, who delivers all sentient beings most excellently, I pray that you take pity on me and grant me the power of mindfulness and wisdom."
He then spoke these *dhāraṇī* verses:

1. Amilajave 2. Haṃ puṣajave 3. Thapanajave 4. Lācāsamī 5. Phaṭarajaśe 6. Sītanaṭave 7. Śirakani 8. Homahoma 9. Mahākālunike svāhā If one wishes to cross the ocean, seek hidden treasures, or seek the path of the immortals;
if one is imprisoned, separated from loved ones, or encounters those who are hateful and hostile;
Whether it be water, fire, knives,
poison, disease, sorcery,
lions, tigers, wolves, venomous snakes, or bandits.
In the face of various fears and for whatever necessities one may require,
that person should invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha,
prostrate before him, and make offerings.
One should conceive of him as a great compassionate father and recite this verse:
“Have mercy on me, have mercy on me, O you renowned for great compassion; Benefactor of the world, Treasury of Space!
I pray that you, with great compassion, look upon me clearly, And rescue me from all such terrors.
O Virtuous One, grant me the benefit of merit; I am now most destitute, oppressed by suffering.
I take refuge in my Honored One, the Great Tranquility; May I obtain happiness in this life and the next.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, manifesting either his own body or the bodies of others in various forms and colors, comforted them, enabling them to attain liberation; furthermore, all necessary items were made fully available to them.

Furthermore, if a prince wishes to succeed to the royal throne, or to the station of a brahmin, a householder, or a craftsman; or to a state of great majesty, great contemplation, or great liberation—he too, during the latter part of the night, shall invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, prostrate, make offerings, and take refuge with a sincere heart.
"The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, with his pure divine ear, hears sounds from afar; he goes before that person and preaches the Dharma for them, causing their wishes to be fulfilled.
'O son of good family!'"
The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha has thus accomplished such inconceivable merit, wisdom, and skillful means.
Even if sentient beings were to count every drop of water in the oceans, they could not know the measure of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha’s merit;
yet there may be sentient beings who can know the limits of the space of the ten directions.

Furthermore, they are unable to know the power of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha’s supernormal transformations and skillful wisdom; for this reason, the light and color of the jewel upon the crown of Ākāśagarbha’s head are thus.
At that time, the assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced with leaping joy, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How can one teach and transform sentient beings within the evil world of the five turbidities?”
The Buddha said, “Good son! It is like space:
without bondage and without liberation, without hatred and without love, its nature is pure.”
"Good son! The Tathāgata is likewise;

having attained mastery over the mind regarding the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), his nature is pure. Although he dwells in a defiled world, he is not stained by worldly dust and grime, appearing in the world for the sake of transforming sentient beings."
"Good son! Does this space abide by depending upon the six consciousnesses? "No, it does not."
“World-Honored One!
Ākāśagarbha addressed the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One!”

Each does not depend upon another, and each has no place of activity; all phenomena are empty and without accumulation. Their primordial limit is as it truly is, like space: without destruction or formation, without recollection or conceptual discrimination, without movement or craving, without son or fruit, without retribution, and without words or letters.
"Bhagavān! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus knows the nature of all dharmas, they attain the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). It is so."
“World-Honored One!
He then spoke the mantra:

“Viparāśa (1) | Maṇḍe’ye (2) | Śenāśaye (3) | Dhyānanimma (4) | Munihara (5) | Anathā (6) | Parākoha (7) | Khepanimma (8) | Abithā (9) | Sūbhaśaśajava (10) | Śanaśana (11) | Śanadathā (12) | Kammaśama (13) | Nimmabuma (14) | Viśaśama (15) | Canda-thāna (16) | Kṛte oṃ puṣpakaṇi svāhā (17). The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent! Son of good family,

you are now able to proclaim this ‘Lion’s Roar Treading upon Water’ Dhāraṇī for Subduing the Eye, which enables all sentient beings at the time of their death to shatter the obstacles of afflictions, the obstacles of karma, and the obstacles of retribution, and to attain rebirth in a Pure Land.”

You are able to take pity on sentient beings and travel through various Buddha-lands, manifesting physical bodies to benefit them, preaching Mahāyāna sūtras that can sever all evils, and causing even the Caṇḍāla kings down to the Caṇḍāla śramaṇas to cultivate all wholesome dharmas.

When the Buddha spoke this sutra, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* beings attained various kinds of samādhis and dhāraṇīs, abided in the various patiences (*kṣānti*), and attained the ten knowledges of the stages;
ten thousand people attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Buddha spoke in verse:
"If sentient beings engage in disputes, they are governed by their fundamental roots;
by being able to master these fundamental roots, one will swiftly behold that [Truth]."
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the entire great assembly rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
*The Sutra of the Divine Incantation of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha*.
